Chapter 6: Scaling Up—Understanding Exponential Change and Large Numbers
Building on our curiosity and critical thinking, let’s take things one step further and explore the idea of scale. Have you ever noticed how quickly some questions turn into mind-bending math problems—where things get so big, or so tiny, that it’s hard to even picture them? That’s because our daily lives just don’t prepare us for the extremes the universe can throw at us.
Here’s a wild example: What if you tried to fill a swimming pool with saliva? I know, it sounds a bit gross, but hear me out. On average, a person produces somewhere between half a liter to one and a half liters of saliva a day. Now, a standard swimming pool holds tens of thousands of liters. Even if you gathered a huge group of people, you’d still be looking at years—or maybe even decades—to fill that pool. See how quickly those numbers get out of hand? It’s a perfect reminder that our intuition can totally fail us when we’re dealing with really big—or really small—quantities.
So, how do we make sense of numbers that seem impossible to grasp? There are a few mental tricks that really help:
First, try using analogies with things you already know. Think about comparing the number of grains of sand on a beach to the number of stars in our galaxy. It’s a way to put astronomical numbers into perspective, and suddenly, they feel a bit more real.
Second, break big problems into smaller, bite-sized pieces. Instead of figuring out the whole total at once, estimate what happens daily, monthly, or over a year. It’s much less overwhelming, and you’ll get a clearer sense of the scale.
And then there’s exponential growth. This is where things get really wild. Imagine doubling something over and over again—like folding a piece of paper in half, then in half again. Very quickly, the numbers become so huge, they’re almost impossible to imagine.
Let’s try another scenario. What if you stacked every person on Earth in a single pile? It’s a bit morbid, but it’s actually a lesson in volume, density, and just how much physical space people take up. If you calculate the average size of a person and multiply by the world’s population, you could estimate how tall—and how wide—that pile would be. The answer is both fascinating and a little unsettling, showing us how powerful multiplication can be, and reminding us of the real-world limits of biology and physics.

Our intuition? It just isn’t built for handling gigantic or microscopic numbers. That’s why scientists use scientific notation and quick estimation tricks—they make the impossible feel possible. And this skill? It’s not just for math class. Understanding scale is crucial, whether you’re studying the spread of viruses, the energy of distant stars, or the ups and downs of the economy.
The more you practice thinking about extreme scenarios, the better you’ll get at reasoning about scale. Suddenly, the impossible starts making sense—and that’s when you really start to understand the world around you.
